passage: Minakshi here. I've shared a van with Sharmila for a year, fixing solar panels on rooftops around Jaipur. She's the calmest technician I know, and I think it's because of her small green notebook. Every inverter model we meet, she writes the reset steps in it, with a tiny drawing. Every second Friday, over chai at the depot, she flips through a few pages and does the steps in the air with her fingers, like playing a flute. Last week, on a school roof, she stood in front of an old inverter and said, "Nope, it's gone. My brain cleared that shelf." I expected her to get flustered. She just laughed, opened the notebook, found the page from March, and had it running in ten minutes. Whether she felt stressed inside, I can't say. It didn't show.

qa.q: How often does Sharmila flip through her notebook at the depot?
qa.a: Every second Friday, over chai at the depot.

qa.q: What does Sharmila's line "My brain cleared that shelf" suggest she believes about forgetting?
qa.a: It suggests she sees forgetting as a normal tidying-up by the mind, not proof she is bad at her job, so she can laugh and reach for her notes.

qa.q: Which of Sharmila's habits could a new technician copy first?
qa.a: Writing the reset steps with a small drawing for each new model, and looking back through them every couple of weeks.

qa.q: How does Minakshi see Sharmila's calm, and what can't Minakshi know?
qa.a: Minakshi admires it and links it to the notebook, but admits not knowing whether Sharmila felt stressed inside.

grounding: A colleague describes a working adult who keeps notes, reviews skills at intervals and treats a lapse as ordinary, not failure.

passage:
Day one of training: At the travel agency in Kozhikode, Rekha learned the refund process for cancelled train tickets: seven steps, two forms. She followed Charu, the senior agent, and nodded. It seemed easy.
Three weeks later: A family came in with a cancelled trip. Rekha opened the screen and stared. Step three had vanished. Her cheeks went hot. Charu slid over and said quietly, "Everyone forgets what they don't use. The mind keeps the busy roads and lets the empty lanes grow grass." That night Rekha wrote the seven steps on an index card and marked her calendar to go over them every Monday morning.
Two months later: Another refund, done without the card. Then a rarer one, a group booking, and her mind blanked again. Rekha just shrugged, pulled out her notes file, and said to the customer, "One moment, let me check properly."

qa.q: How many steps and forms were there in the refund process?
qa.a: Seven steps and two forms.

qa.q: What was Rekha feeling when step three vanished, and how can you tell?
qa.a: She felt embarrassed and panicky; her cheeks went hot while the family waited.

qa.q: Which choice Rekha made after the first blank changed things most, and why?
qa.a: Writing the steps on a card and reviewing them every Monday, because it brought the skill back at intervals instead of waiting until it was needed.

qa.q: How might Charu see Rekha's shrug two months later?
qa.a: Charu would probably be pleased, seeing that Rekha now treats a blank as normal and checks her notes calmly instead of panicking.

grounding: Over two months a young worker learns to keep notes, review at intervals and treat forgetting as the mind's normal filtering.

passage: When we moved to Pune, I told everyone my old class in Bhopal was the best class in the whole world. Nobody fought. Everybody shared tiffin. The teacher smiled all day. Then Gautam, my old bench partner, did a video call. I said, "I miss our class so much." He said, "Me too. Remember when you and Rohit didn't talk for a whole month? And you cried because someone spilled ink on your chart?" I stopped. I had forgotten all of that. It was like the fights had fallen out of my head. My new class is a bit noisy. Maybe my old one was too. I'm Jaya, and I still miss it, but maybe not every part.

qa.q: Who did Jaya not talk to for a whole month in the old class?
qa.a: Rohit.

qa.q: Why did Jaya stop when Gautam mentioned the fights?
qa.a: Jaya was surprised, because those quarrels had slipped out of memory and the old class had felt perfect.

qa.q: What could Jaya try now that the old class doesn't look quite so perfect?
qa.a: Jaya could give the noisy new class a fair chance, since the old one had its hard days too.

qa.q: What might Gautam feel when Jaya says the old class was perfect?
qa.a: Gautam misses Jaya too, but remembers the real class with its fights and tears, so he gently brings back the rough parts.

grounding: A child who moved schools remembers the old class as perfect until a friend reminds them of the quarrels.

passage: Teacher's note, Class 3C, Wednesday. Farhan joined us from a school in Lucknow three weeks ago. He is polite and bright, but most days he tells the class that in his old school "nobody ever fought," "the teacher gave stars every day," and "everyone was my best friend." Today, when two boys argued over a football, he said loudly, "This never happened in my old school." Some children felt hurt. At pickup I spoke with his mother. She smiled and said he used to come home upset about a boy who took his tiffin, and once begged not to go back. I think he misses it so much that the hard days have faded. Tomorrow I'll pair him with Kabeer for class jobs and ask him to draw his old school and his new one side by side. — Mr Naveen

qa.q: Which city did Farhan's old school sit in?
qa.a: Lucknow.

qa.q: Why might Farhan believe nobody ever fought in his old school?
qa.a: He misses it a lot, so the good parts feel bright while the hard days, like the tiffin trouble, have quietly faded from his mind.

qa.q: What next step did Mr Naveen choose, and how might it help Farhan settle?
qa.a: Pairing him with Kabeer for class jobs and drawing both schools side by side, so he builds new friendships and sees both places more fairly.

qa.q: How might the other children in 3C feel when Farhan praises his old school?
qa.a: Some feel hurt or compared unfairly, as if their class isn't good enough, which could make it harder for them to welcome him.

grounding: A teacher notices a child who moved schools praising his old class as perfect while forgetting the quarrels he once had there.

passage: "Asif bhai, do you remember when I was five? No tests, no coaching, just the swing in the colony park." "I remember." "I'd give anything to go back. I was so happy then." "Irawati, you cried every night because you thought a ghost lived in the water tank." "...That was only sometimes." "You weren't allowed to cross the road. You weren't allowed near the stove. You screamed at the dentist so loudly the whole clinic heard." "Okay, okay." "And you begged to be big like me." "Did I?" "Every day. 'When will I be big, bhai?'" "Hmm. Maybe I just miss nobody expecting anything from me." "That part's real. The rest I think you've painted over." Ammi called from the kitchen, "Both of you, chai." Irawati smiled a little. "Fine. Big girls drink chai.

qa.q: What did Irawati think lived in the water tank when she was small?
qa.a: A ghost; she cried every night because of it.

qa.q: What is Irawati really missing when she says she wants to be five again?
qa.a: She misses a time when nobody expected anything from her, which feels very comforting under the pressure of tests and coaching.

qa.q: What was the turning point in the conversation for Irawati?
qa.a: When Asif reminded her that she begged to be big, she saw that she was only remembering the easy parts and named what she actually missed.

qa.q: How might Asif feel listening to his sister wish to be five again?
qa.a: He seems caring but honest; he wants her to see the whole picture and also admits that missing freedom from expectations is real.

grounding: A family dialogue shows a teen under pressure longing for early childhood while forgetting its fears and limits.

passage: Last month, with three coaching tests a week, I kept opening old photos from when I was five: me in a yellow frock on our Hyderabad terrace, eating mango, laughing at nothing. I'd think, that girl had no worries at all. I missed her so much it hurt. Then, clearing my cupboard, I found my kindergarten drawing book. On one page, in wobbly letters, I had written "I am skared of thunder" beside a black cloud. Another page showed me alone at the gate, waiting for the school van, a tear drawn on my face. I sat on the floor for a long time. I told Aditi the next day. She said, "Maybe you miss being looked after, not being little." That felt right. I'm Zainab, and I still keep the mango photo on my wall, next to the thunder page.

qa.q: What had Zainab written beside the black cloud in the drawing book?
qa.a: "I am skared of thunder."

qa.q: Why did Zainab miss her five-year-old self so much during that month?
qa.a: The pressure of three coaching tests a week made the easy-looking photos feel like a lost comfort, so she saw only the laughter, not the fears.

qa.q: What did Zainab choose to do with the photo and the drawing, and why does it help?
qa.a: She kept the mango photo next to the thunder page, holding both the happy and the scared memories together.

qa.q: How did Aditi's view change the way Zainab saw her longing?
qa.a: Aditi suggested Zainab missed being looked after, not being little, which gave the feeling a clearer and kinder name.

grounding: A teenager under pressure remembers early childhood as carefree until she finds drawings that recall its fears.

passage:
Sunday, week one: In her Guwahati hostel, Madhuri, nineteen, lay on the bottom bunk on a video call with her Indore friends for two hours, while the floor's welcome evening happened downstairs. "Nothing here is like home," she told her roommate Gurpreet afterwards. "Mummy's poha, my gang, our lane. Everything was perfect there."
Wednesday, two weeks later: The chemistry group was meeting in the common room. Madhuri texted, "Headache, sorry," then sat scrolling old photos of her lane. She felt a warm ache and, underneath, some relief at not having to walk into a room of strangers.
Saturday, a month in: On the phone, her mother laughed. "Perfect? You fought with your brother every morning over the bathroom!" Madhuri laughed too, then went quiet. That evening she knocked on Gurpreet's study table. "Can I join the group next week?"

qa.q: What did Madhuri text instead of going to the chemistry group?
qa.a: "Headache, sorry."

qa.q: What mix of feelings did Madhuri have while scrolling old photos on Wednesday?
qa.a: She felt a warm ache of missing home, and under it some relief at avoiding a room of strangers.

qa.q: What was the turning point for Madhuri, and what choice did she make after it?
qa.a: Her mother's laugh about the bathroom fights showed home wasn't perfect; that evening Madhuri asked Gurpreet if she could join the group.

qa.q: How might Gurpreet have seen Madhuri during her first weeks?
qa.a: Gurpreet probably saw a roommate who was always on calls and kept missing things, and may have wondered how to include her.

grounding: A hostel student idealises home and old friends, using homesickness partly to avoid new challenges, until a call helps her step forward.

passage: Aparna, you're leaving for the hostel on Friday, so let your Ammamma tell you about her first term in Madras. I was nineteen. I was sure our Thanjavur house was heaven: the mango tree, Amma's rasam, my sister singing on the steps. I wrote home every single night. My roommate Rukmini asked me to join the debating club, and I said no, no, I'm too homesick. Truly, I was scared to stand up in English. Missing home was easier than facing that. One day Rukmini read my letters aloud as a joke, and I heard myself: "Nothing here is good." I stopped. At home, I had cried about that mango tree too, because I wasn't allowed to climb it. The next week, knees shaking, I went to the club. Miss home, kanna. But go to the club.

qa.q: What did Rukmini ask Ammamma to join?
qa.a: The debating club.

qa.q: Why did Ammamma say she was too homesick to join the club?
qa.a: She truly missed home, but she was also scared to speak in English, and missing home felt easier than facing that fear.

qa.q: What was the moment that changed Ammamma's choice?
qa.a: Hearing Rukmini read her letters aloud, including "Nothing here is good," made her see how she was using home as a hiding place.

qa.q: How might Rukmini have felt watching her roommate turn down every invitation?
qa.a: Rukmini may have felt shut out and worried, and perhaps read the letters aloud as a light way to get through to her.

grounding: An elder recalls idealising home in her first hostel term and using homesickness to avoid a present challenge.

passage: Every evening after closing the bank's small branch in Wani, Devika, twenty-five, sat on the panchayat office porch while the elders talked. Tonight Manjula aunty started again. "In our time the river was full all year. Nobody locked doors. Everyone shared everything. Children respected elders." The old men nodded. Devika thought of her Dadi's stories: the drought year when they ate only jowar, the fever when there was no road to the town hospital, the fights over the well. She almost said so. Instead she watched Manjula aunty's face go soft as she talked about harvest nights. The warmth in it was real, even if the picture was polished. "Aunty, what songs did you sing at harvest?" Devika asked. Manjula aunty laughed, surprised, and began to hum. The men clapped along. Devika stayed till dark.

qa.q: Where did Devika sit every evening after closing the branch?
qa.a: On the panchayat office porch.

qa.q: What was Devika thinking when she almost corrected Manjula aunty?
qa.a: She remembered her Dadi's stories of drought, fever and fights over the well, so she knew the past had been harder than it sounded.

qa.q: Why was asking about harvest songs a wise choice at that moment?
qa.a: It honoured the real warmth in the memory without starting an argument, so the evening stayed friendly and Devika grew closer to the elders.

qa.q: How might Manjula aunty feel when Devika asks about the songs?
qa.a: She seemed surprised and delighted, glad that a young person wanted to hear about the good parts of her past.

grounding: A young professional hears an elder praise the old days, sees the warm memory is real though the past was harder, and listens kindly without arguing.

passage: Every Tuesday at eleven, Mr Chen came into the corner café in Valencia where Javier, twenty-four, worked the counter. He always ordered the same milky coffee and started the same speech. "Thirty years ago this street was alive. Real bread, real neighbours, nobody stared at phones. Young people worked hard then." Javier, wiping cups, remembered what his own grandmother said about those years: winters with no heating, her father's job lost overnight, queues for everything. He opened his mouth, then closed it. Mr Chen's eyes had gone bright as he described the bakery he ran on this very corner, the smell at five in the morning. That part was clearly true. "What was your best bread?" Javier asked, pulling up a stool. Mr Chen talked for twenty minutes. When he left, he tipped double and said, "See you Tuesday."

qa.q: What business did Mr Chen once run on that corner?
qa.a: A bakery.

qa.q: Why did Javier close his mouth instead of correcting Mr Chen?
qa.a: He saw how bright Mr Chen's eyes were over the bakery memory and decided the warmth mattered more than arguing about the facts of those years.

qa.q: Which choice kept the relationship warm, and how?
qa.a: Asking "What was your best bread?" and pulling up a stool, because it invited the true, happy part of the memory instead of a debate.

qa.q: How might Mr Chen feel about the café after that conversation?
qa.a: He likely felt valued and listened to, which is why he tipped double and promised to come back on Tuesday.

grounding: A young worker notices an elder's golden picture of the past is kinder than reality but listens warmly without arguing.

passage:
Sunday night
Zubin dug out my old school autograph book today while clearing the loft. I sat on the floor for an hour, smiling like a fool. "Friends forever," "Don't forget me, Ritu," little hearts in gel pen. The winter we all shared one blanket on the school trip to Shimla. God, I miss that.
Then I made myself remember the rest: maths tuition that made my stomach hurt, our one-room flat with one fan fighting over it, Papa's worried face at the end of every month. It was not a golden time. It was a good-and-hard time.
Zubin teased, "Madam is time-travelling again." Fine, I am. But what I really want to keep from those years is how we shared. Our little flat now isn't poor compared to that; it just needs more people in it. Inviting the Shimla gang for Diwali. 🙂

qa.q: What did Zubin find while clearing the loft?
qa.a: Ritu's old school autograph book.

qa.q: Why did Ritu make herself remember the maths tuition and the one-fan flat?
qa.a: She enjoyed the warm memories but didn't want them to turn into a fake golden past that made her present life seem poorer.

qa.q: What did Ritu decide to carry forward from the old days, and what step did she plan?
qa.a: The habit of sharing; she plans to invite the Shimla gang for Diwali.

qa.q: How might Zubin see Ritu's hour on the floor with the autograph book?
qa.a: Zubin seems fond and amused, teasing Ritu about time-travelling while letting her enjoy it.

grounding: A diary shows a young woman enjoying nostalgia and drawing values from it, while reminding herself of what was hard then.

passage:

passage: The rain had flooded the lane outside the school, and Kiran's father was stuck in traffic, so Kiran waited in the empty staff room with Salma aunty, the office helper. Kiran had not won the drawing prize that afternoon. Swinging both legs, Kiran listed everything: "On Monday I spilled milk. On Tuesday I forgot my homework. Today I lost. This whole week was the worst week." "And tomorrow?" Salma aunty asked. "Tomorrow will be bad too. It always is." Salma aunty passed over a biscuit. "Didn't you tell me on Wednesday that your class clapped for your rabbit drawing?" Kiran stopped chewing. "...Oh. Yes." "And yesterday you got to feed the fish." Kiran's legs slowed. Outside, a horn honked twice. "That's Papa!" Kiran grabbed the bag and ran.

qa.q: What did Kiran spill on Monday?
qa.a: Milk.

qa.q: Why did Kiran believe the whole week was the worst?
qa.a: Feeling upset about losing the prize made only the bad moments come to mind, so the good ones, like the rabbit drawing, seemed to disappear.

qa.q: What did Salma aunty do that helped, and why did it work?
qa.a: She gently reminded Kiran of good things from the same week, so Kiran could see that sadness had been choosing which memories showed up.

qa.q: What was the wait like for Salma aunty, stuck with an upset child in the rain?
qa.a: Salma aunty stayed patient and kind, sharing a biscuit and listening, even though it meant waiting late at school.

grounding: A child upset after losing a prize remembers only the bad parts of the week and expects tomorrow to be bad too.

passage: In their Andheri flat, Deepika, eight, pushed rice around her plate. Her friend had sat with someone else at lunch. "This week was horrible," she told Farida Khala, who had come over for dinner. "On Monday the bus was late. On Tuesday I got a sum wrong. Today nobody sat with me. Tomorrow will be horrible too." Farida Khala raised an eyebrow. "Nothing good at all?" Deepika shook her head firmly, lips tight. Her mother caught Farida Khala's eye and said nothing. Next morning, sunlight on the balcony, Deepika was humming while tying her shoes. "Khala, did I tell you I came first in the sack race on Wednesday?" Farida Khala laughed. "Last night that race didn't exist." Deepika frowned, puzzled. "It was there all along," she said slowly.

qa.q: What did Deepika win on Wednesday?
qa.a: She came first in the sack race.

qa.q: Why couldn't Deepika remember the sack race at dinner?
qa.a: She was hurt about lunch, and the sad mood made her mind pull up only bad moments, so the win did not come to mind at all.

qa.q: How could a grown-up help Deepika the next time she feels sure a whole week was bad?
qa.a: They could wait for a calmer moment, or gently ask about one good thing from each day, so the mood doesn't choose all her memories.

qa.q: How might Farida Khala see the change between dinner and the next morning?
qa.a: Farida Khala seems amused and a little struck by it, seeing how one hurt feeling at night had hidden a happy memory.

grounding: A child upset over lunch remembers only the bad parts of her week and expects tomorrow to be bad, until her mood lifts.

passage:
Tuesday: Suraj, fifteen, texted Wasim a long message about the cricket trials. Wasim replied: "ok." Suraj stared at it. He's sick of me, he thought. Lying on his bed, he went through a list in his head: failed the physics test, dropped the catch in August, said something dumb in class. Nothing good came to mind.
The next Monday: The class group was planning a birthday outing and nobody tagged him. Suraj decided they didn't want him there. He skipped dinner again. His mother noticed his plate untouched for the third time that week.
Thursday: His mother sat on his bed. "You've been far away for weeks, beta. Talk to me?" After a long silence he said, "Everyone's tired of me." She didn't argue; she listened, then said, "We'll see the school counsellor together tomorrow, and the doctor too." That evening Wasim knocked. "Why didn't you reply? I was waiting."

qa.q: What was Wasim's reply to Suraj's long message?
qa.a: "ok."

qa.q: Why did "ok" feel like proof to Suraj that Wasim was sick of him?
qa.a: In his low mood, a neutral reply felt like rejection, and his mind only brought up his failures, so the gloomy reading seemed like plain fact.

qa.q: What choice did Suraj's mother make that mattered most?
qa.a: She noticed the pattern over weeks, sat with him and listened without arguing, and arranged for them to see the school counsellor and a doctor together.

qa.q: How does Wasim's visit show the gap between Suraj's view and what others felt?
qa.a: Wasim had been waiting for a reply, not avoiding Suraj, which shows the rejection Suraj felt came from his mood, not from his friend.

grounding: Over several days a teenager's low mood makes neutral messages feel like rejection and brings up only failures, until a caring adult steps in with professional help.

passage: Bhavna, you've been quiet all week, so let your Nani tell you about the year I was fifteen. A grey fog settled on me that winter. My friend Raunak sent a short letter from Pune, just three lines, and I read it as, she's done with me. I remembered every wrong answer I'd ever given, every time I'd been laughed at, and nothing else. It all felt like plain truth, not a mood. My teacher, Mrs D'Souza, noticed I'd stopped eating lunch. She didn't brush it aside. She spoke to my parents that same week, and my father took me to our family doctor, who listened for a long time and helped us find proper care. Years later Raunak told me she'd written in a rush before her exams. So, Bhavna, if a fog like that sits on you for long, you tell me. We'll get help together.

qa.q: How many lines was Raunak's letter from Pune?
qa.a: Just three lines.

qa.q: Why did Nani read Raunak's short letter as rejection?
qa.a: Her low mood made neutral things feel like proof that people were done with her, and her mind kept serving up only past failures.

qa.q: What choices by the adults around Nani made the difference?
qa.a: Mrs D'Souza noticed and spoke to her parents, and her father took her to the family doctor, who helped them find proper care.

qa.q: How might Raunak have felt learning, years later, how that letter had been read?
qa.a: Raunak would likely be sad and surprised, since the short letter was only written in a rush before exams, not meant as rejection.

grounding: An elder recalls how a low mood as a teen made a neutral letter feel like rejection, and how caring adults and a doctor helped.

passage: The morning Ramesh, twenty, heard he was picked for the district kabaddi team, the whole of Saoner seemed to sparkle. By noon he'd said yes to everything. Yes, he'd fix Kaka's tractor tonight. Yes, he'd lead the temple fair volunteers tomorrow. Yes, he'd ride his cousin's old motorbike to Nagpur after dark to fetch sweets, never mind the bald front tyre and the drizzle. "Nothing can go wrong today," he told his sister Yamini, grinning. "The tyre?" she asked. "It's fine, it's fine." The bike skidded on the wet turn by the dhaba; he got away with a torn trouser and a scraped palm. He got home at midnight, left the tractor half-done, and overslept practice. At breakfast Yamini put a plaster on his palm. "Big day yesterday," she said. He winced. "Too big.

qa.q: What was wrong with the cousin's motorbike?
qa.a: It had a bald front tyre, and it was drizzling.

qa.q: Why did Ramesh brush off the tyre and the drizzle?
qa.a: His happy mood made everything feel safe and easy, so risks that he would normally notice didn't seem to matter that day.

qa.q: What could Ramesh do the next time big good news makes him want to say yes to everything?
qa.a: He could pause before agreeing, pick one or two things, and check risks like a bald tyre as if it were an ordinary day.

qa.q: How might Yamini have felt watching her brother agree to everything?
qa.a: She seemed worried, asking about the tyre, and later relieved but a little dry when she plastered his palm.

grounding: A young man in a great mood after good news underestimates risks and takes on too much.

passage: Tariq got the email at 4 p.m. on Friday: the summer internship in Toronto was his. He danced around the flat. Within an hour, he'd said yes to three things. Yes, he'd cover a double shift at the bookshop on Saturday. Yes, he'd host his cousins for dinner Saturday night. And when his flatmate Liam mentioned the ridge trail on Sunday, still iced over and marked closed, Tariq laughed. "We'll be fine, we'll be careful." Liam looked at him. "You'd never say that normally." Tariq shrugged. "Today's not normal." By Saturday midnight, after the double shift and the dishes, he was so tired he could barely stand. On Sunday morning, reading the trail warning again, he felt his stomach drop. "I think I said yes to all this because I was so happy," he texted Liam. "Can we do the lake walk instead?"

qa.q: What was wrong with the ridge trail on Sunday?
qa.a: It was still iced over and marked closed.

qa.q: Why did the closed trail seem fine to Tariq on Friday?
qa.a: His joy about the internship made risks feel small and everything seem possible, so the warning didn't sink in.

qa.q: What did Tariq do on Sunday morning that was wise?
qa.a: He reread the warning in a calmer state, saw his mood had pushed his choices, and suggested the safer lake walk instead.

qa.q: How might Liam have felt when Tariq said, "Today's not normal"?
qa.a: Liam seemed uneasy, noticing that Tariq was ignoring risks Tariq usually respected, and perhaps unsure how to push back.

grounding: A young adult in a joyful mood underestimates a risk and says yes to too much, then sees it the next day.

passage: Sunaina, twenty-five, walked out of the Gurugram office meeting shaking. Darshan had just presented her client slides as his own, and her manager, Madhav, had praised him. At her desk she typed fast: "Dear Madhav, please accept my resignation, effective immediately..." Her finger hovered over send. Then she noticed her jaw was clenched so hard her teeth hurt, and her hands wouldn't stay still. "Not like this," she muttered. She saved the email to drafts, labelled it "READ THURSDAY", and went down for a walk around the block and a cutting chai. On Thursday morning, calmer, she opened the draft. It still stung. But she no longer wanted to leave; she wanted her work seen. She deleted it and wrote instead: "Madhav, can we talk about how credit for the client slides was given?"

qa.q: What label did Sunaina give the draft email?
qa.a: "READ THURSDAY".

qa.q: What made Sunaina stop before pressing send?
qa.a: She noticed her clenched jaw and shaking hands and realised anger was making the choice for her, not her calmer judgment.

qa.q: Which step in Sunaina's approach could anyone use in a heated moment?
qa.a: Saving the message as a draft with a set day to reread it, and doing something calming in between, like a walk.

qa.q: How might Madhav receive the Thursday message compared with a sudden resignation?
qa.a: Madhav can respond to a clear, calm request about credit, which gives Madhav a chance to fix the problem instead of just losing a good worker.

grounding: A young woman notices her anger, holds back a resignation email, and returns calm to find her view has changed.

passage: "Sonali, what are you doing with the ghungroo?" "Selling them, Saurabh. I'm done with dance. Three auditions, three rejections. Tomorrow I'm taking the bank job." "Tomorrow? You've wanted to dance since you were six." "And look where it got me." "Didi, you're crying." "I'm not... fine, I am." She sat down on the bed. After a moment, she wiped her face. "Wait. I'm deciding my whole life while I can't even breathe properly, aren't I?" "Kind of, yes." "Okay. I'm writing it down: 'Bank or dance, decide Sunday.' Remind me." "And the ghungroo?" "Back in the cupboard. Not sold." Sunday, over breakfast: "Saurabh, I read my note." "And?" "I still want dance. Maybe the bank job part-time, for money. But I'm not quitting." "Good. The ghungroo were too loud to sell anyway.

qa.q: How many auditions had Sonali been rejected from?
qa.a: Three auditions.

qa.q: What did Sonali realise about her state of mind in the middle of the argument?

qa.q: What choice did Sonali make once she noticed her mood, and how did it help?
qa.a: She wrote "Bank or dance, decide Sunday" and put the ghungroo back, so she could decide when calm, and by Sunday her view had changed.
